title: Science says your boss should talk less in meetings
gist: Ars Technica (via Knowable Magazine) surveys the growing field of meeting science, fueled by data from archived virtual meetings: leaders who talk less and listen attentively run better meetings, and recurring meetings are often aimless. Yet a 2026 NBER study of 9,000+ Norwegian workers links meeting intensity to wage growth and on-the-job learning.

themes.theme: Scale and cost of workplace meetings

insights.claim: Close to 1 billion meetings take place daily worldwide, and CEOs spend nearly three-quarters of their workdays in meetings.
insights.speaker: Knowable Magazine
insights.so_what: Meetings are a huge sink of executive time, a core productivity lever and a market for meeting-optimization tools.
insights.quote: CEOs spend nearly three-quarters of their workdays in meetings.

insights.claim: Meeting science, once a tiny niche of organizational psychology, is accelerating because archived virtual meetings now provide vast amounts of behavioral data.
insights.speaker: Knowable Magazine
insights.so_what: Recorded virtual meetings are becoming a data asset for workplace analytics and AI products.
insights.quote: The field is accelerating as archived virtual meetings provide vast swaths of data.

insights.claim: Research finds employees anticipate feeling worse and being less productive when their day is packed with meetings, especially when working on complex tasks.
insights.speaker: Knowable Magazine
insights.so_what: Meeting overload is a measurable drag on knowledge-worker productivity.

themes.theme: Leaders should listen more than talk

insights.claim: A video-based study led by Nale Lehmann-Willenbrock found that respectful, attentive inquiry by meeting leaders improved team performance, unlike leaders who asked questions without listening to answers.
insights.speaker: Knowable Magazine
insights.so_what: Management listening behavior is a cheap, evidence-backed driver of team output.
insights.locator: In one experiment, Lehmann-Willenbrock and colleagues

insights.claim: Meeting leaders tend to talk the most, which leads them to overrate their own meetings relative to participants' views.
insights.speaker: Knowable Magazine
insights.so_what: Leadership self-assessment of meeting quality is biased; participant feedback is a better signal.
insights.quote: “Often, leaders talk the most, which is also why they often think their meetings are pretty good,” she says.
insights.locator: The balance of listening and speaking

insights.claim: Habitual self-muting in virtual meetings often eliminates active listening entirely, according to Lehmann-Willenbrock.
insights.speaker: Knowable Magazine
insights.so_what: Remote-work tooling design may undermine collaboration quality.
insights.quote: very often, active listening is killed completely.

insights.claim: Pre-meeting small talk predicts meeting effectiveness, particularly for introverted participants, yet it is rare in virtual meetings, so leaders should institute early arrival or informal check-ins.
insights.speaker: Knowable Magazine
insights.so_what: Simple norms can raise effectiveness of remote meetings at near-zero cost.
insights.locator: Indeed, her studies on face-to-face meetings

insights.claim: Liana Kreamer recommends silent brainstorming (brainwriting) in a shared chat or document, citing a 2009 study that found it more effective than free-for-all spoken brainstorming.
insights.speaker: Knowable Magazine
insights.so_what: Collaborative-document tools can outperform verbal ideation, favoring async/shared-workspace software.

insights.claim: In an unpublished survey of 147 employees, Zofia Walters found people with ADHD reported more virtual meeting fatigue, especially with cameras on for long periods, and poorer emotional states than non-ADHD peers.
insights.speaker: Knowable Magazine
insights.so_what: Camera-on mandates may impose hidden costs on part of the workforce.
insights.locator: In findings yet to be published

insights.claim: Walters' findings suggest multitasking during meetings may help attendees with ADHD manage boredom or hyperactivity.
insights.speaker: Knowable Magazine
insights.locator: In findings yet to be published

themes.theme: Purposeless recurring meetings vs. measurable payoffs

insights.claim: Ava Scott's research on Microsoft employees found recurring meetings tend to be the most aimless, and Kreamer notes that Shopify has cut all recurring meetings.
insights.speaker: Knowable Magazine
insights.so_what: Cutting recurring meetings is a corporate productivity lever being adopted by companies like Shopify.
insights.quote: Kreamer notes that some companies, such as Shopify, have cut all recurring meetings.
insights.locator: Recurring meetings tend to be the most aimless

insights.claim: A 2026 NBER study led by Harvard economist David Deming, covering more than 9,000 Norwegian workers, found meeting intensity positively associated with subsequent wage growth and on-the-job learning, possibly via contact with senior colleagues.
insights.speaker: Knowable Magazine
insights.so_what: Aggressive meeting cuts may sacrifice knowledge transfer and human-capital growth.
insights.quote: found that meeting intensity is positively associated with subsequent wage growth and on-the-job learning.

insights.claim: The Deming study is correlational, but it suggests that while meeting costs are especially high at high-wage companies, the benefits may be even higher.
insights.speaker: Knowable Magazine
insights.so_what: For high-wage firms, meeting time may be an investment rather than pure overhead.
insights.quote: “Meetings are the broccoli of work—widely disliked, but probably good for us anyway.”
insights.locator: The important caveat is that the study

insights.claim: Authentic, positive humor in meetings can spur new ideas and enhance team performance, most likely when participants know each other well, per Lehmann-Willenbrock's analysis of meetings at two German companies.
insights.speaker: Knowable Magazine
insights.so_what: Team familiarity and psychological safety condition creative output.
insights.locator: Humor can help make a meeting successful

insights.claim: Vita Stout's study of the 2022 International Congress for Bat Research found joke-telling was concentrated among older, well-established male scientists rather than early-career and underrepresented researchers.
insights.speaker: Knowable Magazine
insights.so_what: Meeting dynamics can reinforce existing power hierarchies, relevant to culture and DEI outcomes.
insights.locator: But not everyone is comfortable using humor

insights.claim: A survey of 1,432 workers in six countries found respondents from the US and the Netherlands especially perturbed by late leaders, while those from China and Chile were much less bothered.
insights.speaker: Knowable Magazine
insights.so_what: Meeting norms differ across cultures, which matters for multinational management.
insights.locator: Some research suggests there are cultural differences

insights.claim: Most meeting best practices from 30 years of research come from Europe or North America, leaving open whether they apply elsewhere.
insights.speaker: Knowable Magazine
insights.so_what: Western management playbooks may not transfer cleanly to other markets.
insights.locator: There are very few cross-cultural studies
